lesson.title: Close Enough to Straight: The Tangent Line Approximation
lesson.summary: Zoom in far enough on a smooth curve and it looks just like its tangent line, which means the tangent line's height is a fast, accurate stand-in for the curve's height nearby.
lesson.body:
Pick any point on a smooth curve and zoom in close enough, and the curve starts to look straight. The straight line it resembles is the tangent line at that point: the line through (a, f(a)) with slope f'(a), exactly the object linear approximation builds. Because the tangent line touches the curve at x = a and points in the same instantaneous direction the curve is heading at that instant, the two stay very close together for x near a. That closeness is the whole idea behind the tangent line approximation: when f(x) is hard or slow to compute directly, walk along the tangent line instead and read off its height.

The payoff is speed. Square roots, cube roots, and other awkward expressions can be estimated by hand once you know the function's value and slope at one convenient nearby point, without ever touching the actual formula for f at the point you care about.

Here is the idea in action. Let f(x) = sqrt(x), and suppose you want sqrt(4.1) but only know exact values near x = 4. Since f(4) = 2, and f'(x) = 1/(2 sqrt(x)) gives f'(4) = 1/(2*2) = 0.25, the tangent line at x = 4 is y = 2 + 0.25(x - 4). Evaluating that line at x = 4.1 gives y = 2 + 0.25(0.1) = 2.025. The true value of sqrt(4.1) is 2.024845673..., so the tangent line's estimate misses by only about 0.00015, an error smaller than two hundredths of one percent.

That accuracy is not an accident, and it is not guaranteed everywhere either. It works because x = 4.1 is close to a = 4. If you tried to use the same tangent line to estimate something far away, like sqrt(9), the straight line would drift away from the curving square root function and the estimate would get noticeably worse. The phrase "near a" is doing real work in this idea, and the next chapters pin down exactly how the error grows as you move away from it.
